use: Health in general; kenkou ni ii = good for you.

example.romaji: Sore, kenkou ni ii n da yo.
example.ja: それ、健康にいいんだよ。
example.english: That's actually good for your health.

examplePolite.romaji: Sore wa kenkou ni ii n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: それは健康にいいんですよ。
examplePolite.english: That's good for your health, you know.

notes: Also a na-adjective: kenkou na = healthy. 'Take care of yourself' is usually karada ni ki o tsukete.

use: A bit formal; for your own cold people usually say yoku naru or naoru.

example.romaji: Kare, daibu kaifuku shita mitai da yo.
example.ja: 彼、だいぶ回復したみたいだよ。
example.english: He seems a lot better now.

examplePolite.romaji: Kare wa daibu kaifuku shita you desu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はだいぶ回復したようです。
examplePolite.english: He seems to have recovered quite a bit.

notes: Also used for the weather, the economy, or HP in games.

use: You 'pull' a cold: kaze o hiku; kaze hiita = I've caught a cold.

example.romaji: Kaze hiita mitai, nodo ga itai.
example.ja: 風邪ひいたみたい、喉が痛い。
example.english: I think I've caught a cold; my throat hurts.

examplePolite.romaji: Kaze o hiita mitai de, nodo ga itai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 風邪をひいたみたいで、喉が痛いです。
examplePolite.english: I think I've caught a cold, and my throat hurts.

notes: Same sound as kaze (wind); context tells them apart. Kazegusuri = cold medicine.

use: Ninshin shite iru = is pregnant.

example.romaji: Jitsu wa, ninshin shita no.
example.ja: 実は、妊娠したの。
example.english: Actually... I'm pregnant.

examplePolite.romaji: Jitsu wa, ninshin shimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 実は、妊娠しました。
examplePolite.english: Actually, I'm pregnant.

use: Exercise for your health; undou suru = to work out.

example.romaji: Motto undou shinai to dame da na.
example.ja: もっと運動しないとダメだな。
example.english: I really need to get more exercise.

examplePolite.romaji: Motto undou shinai to ikemasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: もっと運動しないといけませんね。
examplePolite.english: I really should exercise more.

notes: Undou busoku = not getting enough exercise. It can also mean a political or social movement.

use: The friendly everyday word; isha alone sounds blunt, and you address a doctor as sensei.

example.romaji: Ichido oishasan ni mite moratta hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: 一度お医者さんに診てもらった方がいいよ。
example.english: You should get a doctor to take a look.

examplePolite.romaji: Ichido oishasan ni mite moratta hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 一度お医者さんに診てもらった方がいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You should have a doctor look at it.

notes: People often say byouin ni iku (go to the clinic) for 'see a doctor'.

use: Always about losing weight; daietto chuu = on a diet.

example.romaji: Ima daietto chuu dakara, amai mono wa ii ya.
example.ja: 今ダイエット中だから、甘いものはいいや。
example.english: I'm on a diet, so I'll pass on sweets.

examplePolite.romaji: Ima daietto chuu na node, amai mono wa kekkou desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今ダイエット中なので、甘いものは結構です。
examplePolite.english: I'm on a diet, so no sweets for me, thanks.

notes: Daietto suru = go on a diet. What you normally eat is shokuji, not daietto.

use: Weight goes up (fueru) or down (heru); taijuu o hakaru = weigh yourself.

example.romaji: Saikin, taijuu ga sankiro mo fueta.
example.ja: 最近、体重が3キロも増えた。
example.english: I've put on a whole three kilos lately.

examplePolite.romaji: Saikin, taijuu ga sankiro mo fuemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 最近、体重が3キロも増えました。
examplePolite.english: I've gained three kilos recently.

english: lack of sleep; not getting enough sleep
use: Often given as the reason you're off: nebusoku de = because I didn't sleep enough.

example.romaji: Nebusoku de atama ga mawaranai.
example.ja: 寝不足で頭が回らない。
example.english: I'm so short on sleep I can't think straight.

examplePolite.romaji: Nebusoku de, atama ga mawaranai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 寝不足で、頭が回らないんです。
examplePolite.english: I haven't slept enough, so I can't think straight.

use: The yearly check-up most companies and schools require.

example.romaji: Raishuu, kaisha no kenkou shindan ga aru.
example.ja: 来週、会社の健康診断がある。
example.english: We've got the company health check next week.

examplePolite.romaji: Raishuu, kaisha no kenkou shindan ga arimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 来週、会社の健康診断があります。
examplePolite.english: There's a company health check next week.

notes: Often shortened to kenshin. Kenkou shindan o ukeru = have a check-up.

use: Means both the person and the clinic: haisha ni iku = go to the dentist.

example.romaji: Ha ga itai kara, ashita haisha ni iku n da.
example.ja: 歯が痛いから、明日歯医者に行くんだ。
example.english: My tooth hurts, so I'm going to the dentist tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: Ha ga itai node, ashita haisha ni ikimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 歯が痛いので、明日歯医者に行きます。
examplePolite.english: I have a toothache, so I'm going to the dentist tomorrow.

notes: Haisha-san is the softer, everyday form.

use: Hanamizu ga deru = have a runny nose.

example.romaji: Kaze kana, hanamizu ga tomaranai.
example.ja: 風邪かな、鼻水が止まらない。
example.english: Maybe it's a cold; my nose won't stop running.

examplePolite.romaji: Kaze kamoshiremasen. Hanamizu ga tomaranai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 風邪かもしれません。鼻水が止まらないんです。
examplePolite.english: It might be a cold. My nose won't stop running.

notes: Hana o kamu = blow your nose; hanazumari = a blocked nose.

use: A common summer warning in Japan; netchuushou ni naru = get heatstroke.

example.romaji: Kyou atsui kara, netchuushou ni ki o tsukete ne.
example.ja: 今日暑いから、熱中症に気をつけてね。
example.english: It's hot today, so watch out for heatstroke.

examplePolite.romaji: Kyou wa atsui node, netchuushou ni ki o tsukete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は暑いので、熱中症に気をつけてください。
examplePolite.english: It's hot today, so please watch out for heatstroke.

use: Very common in Japan each spring; kafunshou nan da = I've got hay fever.

example.romaji: Kafunshou de, me ga kayukute tamaranai.
example.ja: 花粉症で、目がかゆくてたまらない。
example.english: My hay fever's making my eyes itch like crazy.

examplePolite.romaji: Kafunshou de, me ga totemo kayui n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 花粉症で、目がとてもかゆいんです。
examplePolite.english: My eyes are really itchy from hay fever.

notes: Kafun = pollen; sugi (cedar) is the main culprit.

use: Seki ga deru = to cough; seki ga tomaranai = can't stop coughing.

example.romaji: Kinou kara seki ga zenzen tomaranai.
example.ja: 昨日から咳が全然止まらない。
example.english: I haven't stopped coughing since yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: Kinou kara seki ga tomaranai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日から咳が止まらないんです。
examplePolite.english: I've been coughing nonstop since yesterday.

notes: Seki o suru also works. A sneeze is kushami.

use: The police as an organisation; a single officer is keisatsukan, or omawarisan.

example.romaji: Sugu keisatsu ni denwa shite!
example.ja: すぐ警察に電話して！
example.english: Call the police right now!

examplePolite.romaji: Sugu keisatsu ni denwa shite kudasai!
examplePolite.ja: すぐ警察に電話してください！
examplePolite.english: Please call the police right away!

notes: Keisatsu o yobu = call the police (110 in Japan). A kouban is the local police box.

use: A crime or shocking event, as in the news or detective shows; jokingly, any big deal.

example.romaji: Kinjo de jiken ga atta rashii yo.
example.ja: 近所で事件があったらしいよ。
example.english: Apparently something happened in the neighbourhood.

examplePolite.romaji: Kinjo de jiken ga atta rashii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 近所で事件があったらしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Apparently there was an incident in the neighbourhood.

notes: Jiko is an accident; jiken is something people did, often a crime.

use: Used when commenting on how the world or life works.

example.romaji: Yo no naka, sonna ni amaku nai yo.
example.ja: 世の中、そんなに甘くないよ。
example.english: Life isn't that easy, you know.

examplePolite.romaji: Yo no naka wa sonna ni amaku nai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 世の中はそんなに甘くないですよ。
examplePolite.english: The world isn't that easy, you know.

notes: Shakai is society as a system; yo no naka is the world as people live it.

use: An unplanned accident, most often a traffic accident.

example.romaji: Eki no mae de jiko ga atta n datte.
example.ja: 駅の前で事故があったんだって。
example.english: I heard there was an accident in front of the station.

examplePolite.romaji: Eki no mae de jiko ga atta sou desu.
examplePolite.ja: 駅の前で事故があったそうです。
examplePolite.english: I heard there was an accident in front of the station.

notes: Jiko ni au = be in an accident. Jiken is an incident, often a crime.

use: Formal or official permission; kyoka o morau = get permission.

example.romaji: Sore, joushi no kyoka moratta?
example.ja: それ、上司の許可もらった？
example.english: Did you get your boss's okay for that?

examplePolite.romaji: Sore wa joushi no kyoka o moraimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: それは上司の許可をもらいましたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you get your manager's approval for that?

notes: Kyoka suru = to permit. Day to day, people just ask ii? to ask if something's okay.
